Do distinct groups differ? A heterogeneity test before pooling

Source: R/dsc.R
dstntst.Rd

Tests whether the estimates of one indicator for distinct groups (First Nations, Metis and Inuit; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people; any groups with published intervals) differ more than their intervals allow, and says how much of their spread is real: the evidence for reporting each group distinctly rather than as one pooled figure.

Usage

dstntst(
  data,
  grp,
  est,
  lower,
  upper,
  qual = NULL,
  conflvl = 0.95,
  pooled = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'dstntst'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per group.

grp, est, lower, upper

Column names.

qual

Optional column of quality flags; suppressed rows are left out.

conflvl

Confidence level of the published intervals, and the level of the verdict printed (default 0.95).

pooled

Optional labels of rows that pool other groups.

x

A result of dstntst().

...

Not used.

Value

A list of class dstntst: groups (the estimates used, with their standard errors), pooled (the inverse-variance mean) and poose, q, df, p_value, i2, leftout (the rows not used) and conflvl. print() shows it.

Details

With estimates \(y_g\), standard errors \(s_g\) from the published intervals and weights \(w_g = 1/s_g^2\), Cochran's \(Q = \sum w_g (y_g - \bar y_w)^2\) has a chi-squared distribution on \(G - 1\) degrees of freedom when the groups share one value, and \(I^2 = \max(0, (Q - (G-1))/Q)\) is the share of the spread that is real rather than sampling error (Higgins and Thompson 2002). A pooled figure is a weighted mean of different populations whenever \(I^2\) is large; a population-weighted total also depends on how many people are in each group, so it is mostly the largest group's figure. Rows that pool groups are left out (pooled, or labels starting with "Total", "Indigenous identity", "Aboriginal identity", "Total Indigenous" or "Indigenous population"); every other row is included, so drop a reference group yourself, and never test overlapping groups ("alone" beside “alone or in combination”) together: they are not independent. Rows with a quality flag "F", "x", ".." or "..." (suppressed) are left out; other flags than those and "E" are treated as usable, with a warning. An estimate outside its own interval is not compared, with a warning. With two or three groups the test has little power and \(I^2\) is imprecise; a large \(p\) is not evidence that the groups are the same.

References

Higgins, J. P. T. and Thompson, S. G. (2002). Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine 21(11), 1539-1558. doi:10.1002/sim.1186

Examples

# your own table: made-up numbers, with the pooled row named
own <- data.frame(
  group = c("Aboriginal", "Torres Strait Islander", "Both"),
  est = c(24.0, 31.0, 24.6),
  lo = c(22.1, 26.2, 22.8),
  hi = c(25.9, 35.8, 26.4)
)
dstntst(own, "group", "est", "lo", "hi", pooled = "Both")
#> Distinctions test: 2 groups
#>   Cochran's Q 7.06 on 1 df, p = 0.00787
#>   I-squared: 86% of the variation is beyond chance
#>   Pooled: 24.95 (se 0.901, inverse-variance mean)
#>   Left out: Both
#>                   group estimate        se
#>              Aboriginal       24 0.9694056
#>  Torres Strait Islander       31 2.4490246

# simulated victimisation rates of three police divisions
div <- data.frame(
  division = c("North", "Central", "South"),
  rate = c(4.1, 5.3, 4.4), lo = c(3.6, 4.7, 3.9), hi = c(4.6, 5.9, 4.9)
)
dstntst(div, "division", "rate", "lo", "hi")
#> Distinctions test: 3 groups
#>   Cochran's Q 9.42 on 2 df, p = 0.00899
#>   I-squared: 79% of the variation is beyond chance
#>   Pooled: 4.52 (se 0.155, inverse-variance mean)
#>    group estimate        se
#>    North      4.1 0.2551067
#>  Central      5.3 0.3061281
#>    South      4.4 0.2551067
